Une inscription de leurs noms dans un lieu public risque de renforcer ce sentiment de stigmatisation. De plus, les victimes des actes perpétrés par les militaires sont encore en vie. A cet égard, la Commission estime qu'il serait aberrant d'ériger un monument avec l'inscription des noms des victimes d'abus des FARDC. Elle fait suite en revanche à la demande d'ériger un monument avec la mention « Plus jamais ça, les militaires ont le devoir de nous protéger et non de nous humilier », une mesure d'éducation en vue d'éviter de reproduire les erreurs commises dans le passé et de s'engager sur l'avenir.
Les Plaignants demandent que l'Etat défendeur publie à ses frais la décision sur le fond dans un journal officiel du gouvernement dans les six mois suivant la notification de la décision.

La publication d'une décision judiciaire est une procédure connue dans le système de protection des droits de l'homme en matière de réparation. En particulier, la Cour Africaine des Droits de l'Homme et des Peuples a considéré dans de nombreuses décisions que la publication d'une décision judiciaire est une mesure importante de satisfaction des victimes des violations des droits de l'homme. C'est ainsi que par exemple, dans l'affaire Norbert Zongo C/ Burkina Faso, la Cour a exigé au Burkina Faso de publier, dans un délai de six mois à compter de la date de la présente décision : (a) le résumé en français du présent arrêt préparé par le Greffe de la Cour, une fois dans le journal officiel et une fois dans un quotidien national de large diffusion ; (b) le même résumé sur un site Internet officiel de l'Etat défendeur, et l'y maintenir pendant un an. Il convient par conséquent d'accéder à la demande y afférente.
Les Plaignants demandent à la Commission de prendre toute autre mesure qu'elle jugerait nécessaire dans l'intérêt de la justice pour les victimes.

La Commission recommande à la République Démocratique du Congo de s'assurer que la mise en œuvre de la présente décision implique directement les victimes et leurs représentants et de lui rapporter par écrit toutes les mesures entreprises à l'effet de la mise en œuvre de la présente décision dans un délai de 180 jours.

Pour ces motifs, la Commission déclare que : i. Les articles 1, 5, 6, 7(1) (d), 14 et 16 de la Charte africaine des droits de l'homme et des peuples ont été violés ii. Les articles 3 (1), 4(1), 16, et 19 (c) du Protocole à la Charte africaine relatif aux droits des femmes en Afrique ont été violés ; iii. L'article 14 (2) (a) du Protocole à la Charte africaine relatif aux droits des femmes en Afrique n'a pas été violé.

En conséquence, la Commission recommande à la République Démocratique du Congo de : a) Poursuivre et punir les auteurs des violations dans un délai de six mois courant dès la notification de la décision sur le fond, et veiller à l'exécution immédiate de l'Arrêt RP 003/2013 de la Cour Militaire Opérationnelle du 5 mai 2014. L'exécution se fera sans préjudice des recommandations ultérieures émises par la Commission africaine. b) Mettre en place une Commission en charge d'identifier les vraies victimes des exactions commises par les militaires dans la présente affaire, évaluer le préjudice subi et leur accorder une réparation monétaire adéquate conformément aux procédures nationales. c) Offrir un soutien médical et psychologique ou psychiatrique gratuit et immédiat, adéquat et effectif, par le biais des institutions spécialisées de santé publiques aux victimes qui en feront la demande. d) Inclure un module sur les droits humains dans le curriculum de formation des militaires, des magistrats dans les juridictions militaires, en mettant un accent particulier sur les droits des femmes et particulièrement la protection des femmes/ filles contre les violences sexuelles lors des conflits armés. e) Présenter des excuses publiques aux victimes dans un délai de six mois suivant la notification de la décision dans un événement public largement diffusé sur les ondes d'une station médiatique couvrant tout le territoire national. f) Eriger un mémorial à Minova avec le slogan : « Plus jamais ça, les militaires ont le devoir de protéger la population civile et non de l'humilier ». g) Publier à ses frais la décision sur le fond dans un journal officiel du gouvernement dans les six mois suivant la notification de la décision. h) S'assurer que la mise en œuvre de la présente décision implique directement les victimes et leurs représentants. i) Lui rapporter par écrit, dans les cent quatre-vingt jours (180) jours de la notification de la présente décision, quant aux mesures entreprises à l'effet de la mise en œuvre de la présente décision. Adoptée par la Commission Africaine des Droits de l'Homme et des Peuples lors de sa 80 Session Ordinaire tenue virtuellement du 24 juillet au 2 août 2024

The Secretariat of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Secretariat) received on 3 October 2018 a Communication submitted by the Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa (IHRDA) and the Association of Women Lawyers Defenders of Human Rights (the Complainants), on behalf of 1016 persons (the victims), including 837 women and 179 men.

The persons cited above (hereinafter referred to as "victims"), all of Congolese nationality, are those against whom the violations were committed and on whose behalf the present complaint was submitted.

The Complaint was submitted against the State of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) (hereinafter referred to as the Respondent State or the DRC), a State that ratified the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (the African Charter) on 20 July 1987 and the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights on the Rights of Women in Africa (Maputo Protocol) on 9 June 2008.

The Complainants indicate that these human rights violations against the victims were perpetrated by soldiers of the Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC) between 20 November 2012 and 2 January 2013, in the midst of an armed conflict pitting them against the M23 rebels in North Kivu Province. These violations concern in particular acts of abuse resulting from widespread and systematic looting, torture, intentional serious assault and battery, destruction and extortion of property, armed robbery, death threats, ill-treatment and particularly violent abuse against persons who tried to oppose the violation of their property and the rape of their wives or daughters.

The Complainants report that, following these events, several victims braved the fear of reprisals and lodged a complaint before the Military Prosecutor's Office (Auditorat Militaire) of South Kivu so that the perpetrators, who are well identified and known, would answer for their acts and be punished in accordance with Congolese law.

The Complainants report that, in November 2012, in the midst of the armed conflict, Congolese soldiers decided to flee in the face of the advance of the M23 fighters who had taken the city of Goma, located in the north-eastern part of the DRC. They took the road to Minova, a large village situated on the volcanic shores of Lake Kivu on the border between the North and South Kivu Provinces, where they redeployed.

It emerges from the Complainants' submission that, on the road leading them to Minova-centre, passing through the camps of war-displaced persons and the neighbouring villages of Ndosho, Sake, Shasha, Mubambi, Bweremana, Bwisha, Bunagana, Mubimbi, Kashinji, Katoko, Ruchunda, Kalungu, Mushaki, Kirwa, Bungulube, Buragiza, the FARDC soldiers, furious, humiliated and demoralised, embarked on a destructive rampage lasting more than 10 days, with the following harmful consequences: rape, acts of torture, intentional homicides, attacks against civilians, sexual violence, systematic looting of houses, kiosks and livestock, extortion of property, destruction of property, large-scale armed robbery, illegal occupation of land belonging to rural communities, and the damage of fields and dwellings belonging either to residents, or to war-displaced persons settled in makeshift camps, or to civilians fleeing the war.

According to the victims' statements, the perpetrators of these massive human rights violations were approximately 6,000 to 8,000 soldiers belonging to FARDC units that were fighting the M23 rebels in November 2012 in North Kivu and that had fled towards MINOVA and its surroundings around mid-November 2012. These units are the following: - The 804 and 810 Regiments, the 391 and 41 Commando Regiments and Battalions of the 8th Military Region of North Kivu; the 10062 Battalion of the 10th Military Region of South Kivu sent as reinforcement; the soldiers of the 802 Regiment and the soldiers of the 82 Sector; and the Republican Guard. This first group was deployed to defend the Goma airport. They held their positions in Goma until 19 November 2012 and then fled towards Minova. - The 393 Commando Battalion, under the operational command of the 8th Military Region. This group was sent on an operational mission to Minova in order to establish control in the event that the M23 launched an attack from the territory of Masisi.

The Complainants add that a few months after the partial withdrawal of the FARDC troops to Minova, the Congolese State successively sent there the Senior Military Prosecutor's Office (Auditorat Supérieur) of North Kivu and that of South Kivu to initiate joint investigations into all these human rights violations perpetrated in Minova and the surrounding villages. Begun around the end of November 2012, the pre-trial judicial investigations were closed at the level of the operational Military Prosecutor's Offices in April 2013. They were interrupted many times on the ground that the soldiers under prosecution had all gone to other fronts to fight the M23 and that they had to be heard in order to open the files against them.

The Complainants report that the Military Prosecutor's Offices of South and North Kivu constituted a single file after pre-trial investigation under No. RMP 0372/BBM/013, which was transmitted to the selected defendants at the end of a partial investigation that excluded the real perpetrators of the crimes, thousands of remote victims as well as a dozen martyred villages and dismantled displaced persons' camps that suffered harm, such as MINOVA. They reiterate that this file contained contradictory referral decisions and incomplete and unintelligible minutes drawn up by Military Prosecutors inexperienced in investigating human rights violations, who did not understand the victims' dialects and who feared for their own safety.

The file was transmitted for scheduling on 5 November 2013, that is after 12 months of waiting, to the registry of the Operational Military Court of North Kivu, which had territorial jurisdiction and which entered the case under No. RP003/2013 MP and PC (1016) v. Nzale Nkumu Ngandu and 38 others/Minova-Bweremana.

They report that all the officers prosecuted, with the exception of one, were charged with rape, looting and homicide as war crimes committed by troops placed under their orders. Several other charges were brought against the 25 rank-and-file soldiers (soldiers who are not officers), including war crimes of rape and looting. During the trial, all the parties were validly represented: the Congolese State, civilly liable, was represented by its lawyers and the victims were represented and/or assisted by the group of their counsel funded by the NGOs American Bar Association and Lawyers Without Borders. The defendants, for their part, were represented by their lawyers funded by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP). The Operational Military Court conducted the investigation for 5 months, starting on 20 November 2013.

The Complainants report that it was after a long wait for the verdict that the Operational Military Court (OMC) delivered Judgment RP 003/2013, after 2 years and 5 months of proceedings from December 2012 to May 2014. The judgment was delivered on 5 May 2014 in Goma, in the presence of only a few defendants and in the absence of the victims or their lawyers. Of the 39 accused, only two low-ranking soldiers were found guilty of having committed rape as an ordinary crime. The 14 senior officers, the Chief of Staff of the Land Forces or the Company Commanders who bore responsibility as superiors of the troops from Goma to Minova and its surroundings as a whole, were cleared of all charges although, during their hearings, some of them had confessed. The 9 other junior officers who had also been charged with serious acts of systematic sexual violence were all acquitted. In total, there were 23 acquittals and only 16 convictions of certain rank-and-file soldiers who were found guilty of looting as a war crime.

This OMC judgment was never served on the civil parties who had duly joined the proceedings. It should also be noted that this judgment is not open to appeal or objection in accordance with Article 87 of Law No. 023/2002 of 18 November 2002 on the Military Judicial Code, which provides that: "judgments delivered by the Operational Military Courts are not open to any remedy", a provision supplemented by the Presidential Order which established and authorised ex officio this Operational Court in the operational zones of North Kivu. In other words, the victims, who are very dissatisfied with Judgment RP 003/2013, can neither appeal nor object because this judgment was delivered at first and last instance.

The Complainants state that this complaint has not been submitted to another international body for the settlement of disputes or having similar competence in accordance with Article 56(7) of the African Charter.

The Complainants allege the violation of Articles 1, 4, 5, 6, 7, 14, 16 and 16 of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (the African Charter) and Articles 3, 4, 8, 11, 14, 24 and 25 of the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights on the Rights of Women (the Maputo Protocol).

The Complainants request the Commission to: a. Examine the present Communication pursuant to Articles 55 and 56 of the African Charter. b. Find that the Congolese government is guilty of violations of Articles 1, 5, 6, 7, 14 and 16 of the African Charter and Articles 3, 4, 11, 14, 16 and 19 of the Maputo Protocol. c. Hold the Congolese State responsible for the acts committed by its agents and order it to make reparation for all the harm caused by them. d. Enjoin the Congolese government to prosecute and punish the perpetrators of the violations in accordance with the Congolese Penal Code.
The Complaint reached the Secretariat of the African Commission on 3 October 2018, which acknowledged receipt of it the same day.

At its 63rd Ordinary Session held from 23 October to 13 November 2018 in Banjul, The Gambia, the Commission considered the Complaint and decided to admit it. On 16 November 2018, the Secretariat informed the parties of this decision and requested the Complainants to submit their arguments on the admissibility of the Communication, in accordance with Rule 105(1) of the Commission's Rules of Procedure (2010).

On 22 January 2019, the Secretariat received from the Complainants a request for an extension of the time limit for submitting their observations on admissibility. The Secretariat informed the Complainants that a period of one month had been granted to them in accordance with the provisions of Rule 113(2) of the Commission's Rules of Procedure (2010).

On 22 February 2019, the Complainants transmitted to the Secretariat their observations on admissibility. On the same date, the Secretariat transmitted the said observations to the Respondent State and requested its response within sixty (60) days. As the Respondent State had not complied with this time limit, the Secretariat notified it that it had a final period of thirty (30) days to submit, failing which the Commission would render a decision by default.

At its successive sessions held between April 2019 and April 2022, the Commission considered the Communication and decided to defer its decision on Admissibility owing to the Respondent State's failure to submit. The required correspondence was sent to the Parties.

At its 71st Ordinary Session held virtually from 21 April to 13 May 2022, the Commission considered the Communication and declared it admissible by default. The Parties were informed thereof and the Complainants' observations on the merits were requested within the time limits provided for by the Rules of Procedure.

At its 72nd Ordinary Session held virtually from 19 July to 2 August 2022, the Commission considered the Communication and decided to defer its decision on the merits pending the observations of the parties. This decision was communicated to the parties on 13 August 2022 and the Complainants' observations were requested.

On 07 October 2022, the Complainants requested an extension of thirty (30) days in order to finalise the arguments on the merits. On 16 November 2022, the Commission granted them an additional period of thirty (30) days. The Respondent State was duly informed on the same date.

On 15 December 2022, the Complainants transmitted to the Secretariat their observations on the merits. On 16 December 2022, the Secretariat acknowledged receipt thereof and transmitted the said observations to the Respondent State and requested its response within sixty (60) days.

At its 74th Ordinary Session held from 21 February to 7 March 2023, the Commission decided to defer consideration of the Communication to a later session pending the arguments of the Respondent State. The Secretariat notified the parties on 16 March 2023 and a reminder was sent to the Respondent State.

At the 75th Ordinary Session held from 3 to 23 May 2023, in Banjul, The Gambia, the Commission deferred the matter again for the same reasons. The Secretariat notified the parties on 5 June 2023. On the same occasion, the Respondent State was informed that it had a final period of thirty (30) days to submit its observations on the merits, failing which the Commission would render a decision by default. At the expiry of the said period, the Respondent State had still not submitted its observations.
At its subsequent sessions, the Commission deferred consideration of the Communication owing to time constraints.

Relying on the observations they submitted for that purpose, the Complainants argue that the Communication fulfils the requirement set out in Article 56(1) since the identity of the authors of the Communication is indicated. The Communication is submitted by two non-governmental organisations (NGOs), namely the Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa (IHRDA) and the Association of Women Lawyers Defenders of Human Rights (AFADDH), whose contact details and fields of action are clearly specified in the complaint and on the cover page of their submission on admissibility.

The Complainants also state that the provision of Article 56(2) of the African Charter has been satisfied since the Communication is compatible with the principles set out in the Constitutive Act of the Union and in particular aims at respect for the principles of equality between men and women, respect for human rights in general, the rule of law, the promotion of social justice, respect for human life as well as the condemnation and rejection of impunity. They also argue that the Communication concerns violations of rights recognised by the African Charter and the Maputo Protocol to which the DRC is a party.

The Complainants also assert that the Communication complies with Article 56(3) of the African Charter since it contains no disparaging language either towards the Respondent State and its institutions or towards the African Union and its organs.

With regard to Article 56(4) of the African Charter, the Complainants state that the Communication is not based on news disseminated through the mass media. They argue that their data and arguments are verified and verifiable because they were gathered by one of the Complainants, an NGO based in the DRC, which worked closely with the victims and represented them before the national courts. The Complainants further report that their arguments are corroborated by the reports of several organisations, notably the United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUSCO), the Open Society Initiative for Southern Africa (OSISA) and Human Rights Watch (HRW).

On the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies under Article 56(5) of the African Charter, the Complainants consider that this requirement has been met. They argue that the Operational Military Court seized was the only domestic judicial remedy available to the victims because its decisions are open neither to appeal nor to cassation.

Concerning Article 56(6) of the African Charter, the Complainants indicate that the Communication was submitted within a reasonable time. They stress that, because of the permanent insecurity in North Kivu, which is still prey to armed conflicts, and the vulnerability and destitution of the civil parties, the victims or their representatives could not freely contact the Operational Military Court to inquire about the fate of their case.

The Complainants indicate that the Operational Military Court delivered in May 2014 a decision which could not be formally served on the victims, who were left to their own devices in a volatile security environment unfavourable to the enjoyment of their fundamental rights and freedoms and still under the control of the FARDC, including those very persons who were acquitted or who were never troubled by the military court.

The Complainants report that it was only on 7 February 2018 that the victims were able to get hold of the certified true copy of the Judgment delivered by the High Military Court in May 2014, which until then was considered, at least by the victims, not to have been publicly delivered, much less enforced, even as regards the sanctions imposed on a symbolic number of FARDC members who were ordered to pay damages jointly with the Congolese State held civilly liable.

Basing themselves on the European system for the protection of human rights, the Complainants observe that the service of a decision by a court has an important place in determining reasonable time, which starts to run only from the date on which the applicant and/or his or her representative has sufficient knowledge of the final decision at the domestic level. They therefore argue that the Communication was submitted to the African Commission within a reasonable time.

The Complainants also justify the time taken to seize the Commission by the fear of reprisals, because the victims could not galvanise themselves to seek justice in a context where the sword of Damocles continues to hang over them, thereby increasing their fear of reprisals.

The Complainants further submit that the present Communication concerns a case of massive and continuing violations due to the absence of effective mechanisms to guarantee the accountability of the FARDC for the many human rights violations committed against the victims, notably the rapes, sexual violence and looting of the property of persons concentrated in displaced persons' camps since the events of Minova and surroundings.

The Complainants request the Commission to declare the present communication admissible for purposes of equity and justice, in order to give the 1016 victims of massive human rights violations an opportunity to be heard by it as a mechanism guaranteeing effective protection of their rights, unlike an operational military court which hears cases involving civilians and soldiers, thus becoming both judge and party.

Concerning Article 56(7) of the African Charter, the Complainants state that the violations at issue in the present communication have not been the subject of litigation before other international mechanisms.
The Complainants conclude that the Communication satisfies all the requirements for admissibility and invite the Commission to declare it admissible.
As the procedure shows, the Respondent State has not submitted its observations on the admissibility of the Communication despite the multiple requests made to that effect by the Secretariat.

Article 56 of the African Charter lists seven admissibility requirements that must be cumulatively fulfilled for a Communication to be declared admissible. Noting that the Respondent State has not submitted its observations, the Commission will therefore decide by default, for lack of submissions from it.

Article 56(1) provides that the identity of the author of the Communication must be clearly indicated, even if the author requests the Commission to keep his or her identity anonymous. In the present case, the identity of the authors is clearly indicated. They are the Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa and the Association of Women Lawyers Defenders of Human Rights, which represent 1016 victims, including 837 women and 179 men. The Commission notes that the authors have, in addition to their identities, also provided their addresses and contact details. It concludes that this requirement is met.

In accordance with the provisions of Article 56(2) of the African Charter, the Communication must be compatible with the Constitutive Act of the African Union and the African Charter. The Commission affirmed in the case of Law Society of Zimbabwe v Zimbabwe that the compatibility of a Communication with the Constitutive Act of the African Union rests on its compatibility with the objectives and principles enshrined in the Act, and more specifically on the question whether the claims of the Communication would not contravene the objectives or principles expressed in the Act. In this regard, the Commission notes that neither the arguments nor the requests contained in the Communication infringe any of the principles adopted under the Constitutive Act of the African Union.

As to the requirement of compatibility with the African Charter, the Commission recalls that this principle presupposes that four conditions must be fulfilled. The Communication must allege that a provision of the Charter has been violated (ratione materiae) and must target a State Party and be submitted by an author having standing (ratione personae); the alleged violation must fall within the territorial sphere covered by the Charter (ratione loci) and must be based on events that occurred during the period of application of the Charter in respect of the State (ratione temporis), except where there is evidence of a continuing violation.

The Commission notes that in the present case, the Communication is submitted against the DRC, a State Party to the African Charter, and that the Complainants have standing. It further notes that the Complainants allege the violation of the rights protected by Articles 1,4, 5, 6, 7, 14, 15 and 16 of the Charter and Articles 3, 4, 8, 11, 14, 24 and 25 of the Maputo Protocol. The Commission also notes that the African Charter and the Maputo Protocol were in force in the DRC at the time of the facts. The Commission notes that the Respondent State has been a party to the African Charter since 20/07/1987 and to the Maputo Protocol since 09/06/2008. It further notes that the violations alleged in this communication date from 2012 and therefore post-date the DRC's ratification of the above-mentioned instruments. Accordingly, the Commission concludes that the Communication complies with the provisions of Article 56(2) of the African Charter.

Article 56(3) of the African Charter provides that Communications shall be considered if they are not written in disparaging or insulting language directed against the State concerned and its institutions or the Organization of African Unity. On compliance with these provisions, the Commission notes that the Complainants have not used any language of this nature. It follows that this requirement has been fulfilled.

Under Article 56(4), Communications must not be limited to gathering exclusively news disseminated through the mass media. On this point, the Commission notes that the information submitted by the Complainants is based mainly on the results of field work which enabled them to be in contact with the victims and to collect their testimonies, whose statements were placed on the file. It concludes that the requirement under consideration has been met.

Article 56(5) of the African Charter requires that the Communication be sent after exhausting local remedies, if any, unless it is obvious to the Commission that the procedure of achieving these remedies is unduly prolonged.

The Commission has recalled in its jurisprudence that the purpose of the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies is to enable the State concerned to address in the first instance, under its domestic law, the alleged human rights violation before it is examined by an international body, so as to prevent such a body from being used as a court of first instance and rather to make it a body of last resort.

The Commission notes that the Operational Military Court delivered its decision on the facts of the present Communication in May 2014. The Commission further notes that this decision brought the proceedings to an end at the domestic level since no other court could any longer be seized by the victims concerned. It observes that the decisions of the Operational Military Court are not open to appeal, in accordance with Article 87 of Law No. 023/2002 of 18 November 2002 on the Military Judicial Code and Presidential Order No. 08/003 of 09 January 2008 on the establishment of a Military Court, notably in the operational zones of North Kivu. The Commission concludes that local remedies have been exhausted and that the requirement set out in Article 56(5) has been fulfilled.

According to the wording of Article 56(6) of the Charter, the Communication must be submitted within a reasonable time from the date local remedies were exhausted or from the date the Commission is seized of the matter.

In the present Communication, it emerges from the analysis of Article 56(5) made in the preceding paragraphs that local remedies have been exhausted because the Operational Military Court delivered a decision that is not open to any remedy.
The Commission recalls that the requirement under Article 56(6) aims to instil reasonable diligence and vigilance and to discourage future Complainants from delaying in seizing the Commission.

Although the African Charter does not specify the meaning of the notion of "reasonable time" for submitting a complaint after the exhaustion of local remedies, the Commission, drawing inspiration from the practice in the inter-American and European human rights systems, decided in the case of Majuru v. Zimbabwe that a period of six months may be considered a "usual standard". It recalls, however, its jurisprudence according to which the determination of "reasonable time" for submitting a Communication must be made on a case-by-case basis, according to the circumstances of each case. Thus, the Commission found that 2 years and 5 months in the case of Darfur Relief and Documentation Centre v. Sudan and 1 year and 3 months in the case of Dr Farouk Mohamed Ibrahim v. Sudan were not reasonable periods for seizing it, on the ground that the Complainants had submitted the communication well after the moment that could have been considered reasonable and also gave no sufficient reason for the long wait before seizing the Commission.

By contrast, in the case of Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa and others v. DRC, the Commission considered that the period of three years taken before seizing it was justified, in view of the reasons advanced by the Complainants, namely the physical inaccessibility of the courts, the failure to serve the judgment of the High Military Court as well as the serious and massive nature of the alleged violations.

The Complainants indicate that the present Communication was submitted within a reasonable time because of the insecurity that prevailed in Minova, the failure to serve the decision rendered and the fear of reprisals by the FARDC. They further stress the massive and continuing nature of the alleged violations and the need for fair justice for the victims.

The Commission notes that the violations alleged in the present Communication occurred during the period from November 2012 to January 2013. The victims lodged a complaint before the military prosecutor's office and the investigation file was transmitted to the Operational Military Court of North Kivu on 5 November 2013. The Commission further notes that a judgment not open to appeal was delivered on 5 May 2014 without the presence of the victims who had joined the proceedings as civil parties. It also notes that the victims never received notification and learned of the judgment, informally, only on 7 February 2018. The Commission notes that the Complainants submitted their Complaint on 3 October 2018, that is 4 years and 6 months after the delivery of the final judgment and 7 months after getting hold of the copy of the judgment. It is therefore for the Commission to examine, in light of the arguments advanced by the Complainants, whether or not the time taken to seize it is reasonable.

On the argument based on the climate of insecurity that prevented the Complainants from pursuing their complaint at the national level, the Commission finds that, clearly, the environment of insecurity existing in Minova at the time of the facts, owing to the presence of armed rebel groups, was not conducive to the victims regularly pursuing their complaint with a view to the protection of the law before the authorities implicated in the alleged violations.

On the failure to serve the decision, the Commission notes that the decisions of the Operational Military Court are not open to appeal and entail exhaustion of local remedies. It observes that the failure to serve constitutes a material impediment because it creates a situation likely to delay the seizure of the Commission by the Complainants. Indeed, the Commission is of the view that without notification, the Complainants remain in doubt not only as to the outcome of the proceedings, but also as to the reasons for the decision rendered.

As to the argument based on the fear of reprisals, the Commission is of the view that where the Complainant was unable to seize the courts for fear for his or her life or that of his or her relatives, he or she should be exempted from exhausting local remedies. In the present Communication, considering that acts of reprisal were commonplace in the eastern part of the DRC, it would have been unreasonable and risky to require the Complainants to expose themselves to threats and attacks on their physical integrity by regularly following up on the progress of their complaint lodged before the Operational Military Court. Such a course of action would have been risky for the Complainants who lived in the same community as their tormentors.

With regard to the need for justice and equity owing to the fact that the alleged violations constitute massive and continuing violations of the rights guaranteed by the Charter, the Commission has already had recourse to this factor to justify its decision in the case of Darfur Relief and Documentation Centre v. Sudan. It then decided that, while the purpose of Article 56(6) is to discourage delay in seizing it, it is also its responsibility to offer the Complainant the opportunity to be heard where valid and relevant reasons have justified such a delay.

The Commission notes that the present case concerns allegations of human rights violations committed by soldiers belonging to FARDC units who, in their pursuit of the M23 rebels who had fled to MINOVA, are said to have run amok against the civilian population, committing serious abuses and human rights violations against men, women and children, notably: rapes, sexual violence, acts of torture, intentional homicides, attacks against civilians, systematic looting of houses and kiosks and theft of livestock, extortion and destruction of property. The Commission further notes that 1016 victims lodged a complaint and that they did not obtain justice at the national level despite the exhaustion of local remedies.

The Commission has already concluded that the factor of the "need for fair justice" becomes crucial in situations where the Complainant alleges that local remedies did not meet the imperative of equity and justice that must characterise any procedure aimed at protecting the human rights guaranteed by the African Charter. In the present case, the Complainants invoke the ineffectiveness of the domestic proceedings before an operational military court which hears cases involving civilians and soldiers, thus becoming both judge and party, and the importance of giving the 1016 victims an opportunity to be heard by the Commission as a mechanism guaranteeing effective protection of their rights.

In these circumstances, the Commission considers that the case deserves to be examined on the merits. Indeed, the initial Complaint and the subsequent submissions contain sufficient information to offer the Complainants the opportunity to be heard on the merits. In addition, in view of the gravity of the reported violations and the number of victims, the present Communication manifestly concerns a case of massive human rights violations. In the Commission's view, the massive nature of the violations reinforces the need to guarantee the principles noted above and consequently requires that the case be examined on the merits to avoid any risk of denial of justice in a case of such serious allegations.

The Commission considers that not admitting the present Communication would amount to denying the Complainants the possibility of remedying the lack of equity and justice of which they claim to have already been victims before the domestic courts. In these circumstances, the Commission finds that the time taken by the Complainants to seize it is not unreasonable. The Commission observes that as soon as the Complainants learned of the judgment, albeit unofficially, they seized the Commission 7 months later. The Commission concludes that the Communication fulfils the requirement set out in Article 56(6) of the African Charter.

Finally, under the provisions of Article 56(7), the Communication must not deal with cases which have been settled in accordance with the principles of the Charter of the United Nations, the Constitutive Act of the African Union or the African Charter. The Commission recalls that these provisions require the Communication to respect the principles of res judicata or the authority of a final judgment; of non-lis pendens; and of non bis in idem.

The Commission relies on the elements submitted by the Complainants to find that the Communication does not concern a case that has already been decided by another international or regional human rights body, nor has the case been settled before another forum applying the principles recalled above. It therefore deduces that the requirement set out in Article 56(7) has been respected.
In view of the foregoing, the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights declares the present Communication admissible in accordance with the provisions of Article 56 of the Charter.

The Complainants allege the violation of the right not to be subjected to torture and cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment and of the right to respect for human dignity protected respectively by Article 5 of the African Charter and Article 3.1 of the Maputo Protocol.

The Complainants indicate that, in withdrawing towards Minova Centre passing through the displaced persons' camps and the villages of Ndosho, Sake, Shasha, Mubambiro, Bweremana, Bwisha, Bunagana, Mubimbi, Kashinji, Katoko, Ruchunda, Kalungu, Mushaki, Kirwa, Bungulube, Buragiza, the FARDC soldiers committed in particular gang rape, attacks against civilian populations, sexual violence, systematic looting of houses, kiosks and livestock; extortion and malicious destruction of property, large-scale armed robbery, illegal occupation of land belonging to communities, as well as the damage of fields and dwellings.

The Complainants report that these attacks by FARDC soldiers caused injuries to the bodily and psychological integrity of these populations, as attested by the statements of the victims and the psychologists' reports placed on file in the present Communication.
They argue that such acts by the FARDC, whose responsibility it is to secure the country and its citizens, infringe the dignity of the victims and plunge them into suffering and personal indignity.

The Complainants allege the violation of their right to security. They indicate that during their withdrawal from the city of Goma to the Commune of Minova, the FARDC sowed insecurity along their path in the displaced persons' camps and in the villages between Goma and Minova. They argue that the acts of violence by the FARDC, which targeted essentially women by subjecting them to sexual violence including gang rape, went almost unpunished, leaving the victims in insecurity and at the mercy of soldiers who enjoy this impunity.

They further allege that the individual and gang rapes as well as the systematic looting and destruction of property caused injuries to the bodily and psychological integrity of the populations, as demonstrated by the statements of the victims and the psychologists' reports placed on file.

The Complainants allege the partiality that characterised the judicial proceedings concerning their case. They indicate that after the partial withdrawal of the FARDC from MINOVA, the Senior Military Prosecutor's Office of North Kivu and that of South Kivu initiated, from November 2012 to April 2013, joint investigations into the human rights violations perpetrated in MINOVA and the surrounding villages.

They report that a single file, after a botched pre-trial investigation, included 39 defendants (including 14 senior FARDC officers) out of the 8000 soldiers who had taken part in the operations in Minova and its surroundings.

They allege that the partiality of the military courts in a case involving civilians also manifested itself during the trial phase. According to the Complainants, at the end of the trial, only 16 convictions of certain rank-and-file soldiers were pronounced, and all the officers who commanded the units, including the Chief of Staff of the Land Forces in North Kivu or the Company Commanders, were acquitted.

The Complainants also allege that the partiality of the Operational Military Court manifested itself on the day the judgment was delivered. According to the Complainants, at the time of delivering Judgment RP 003/2013 on 5 May 2014 in Goma, only a few defendants were present and there was a total absence of the victims and their lawyers, to whom the date of the judgment had not been communicated. They argue that the Judgment was moreover not served on the civil parties who had duly joined the proceedings.

The Complainants further allege that to date, the compensation granted by Judgment RP 003/2013 delivered on 5 May 2014, which ordered the DRC in solidum to pay a compensation of USD 15,000 per victim to a very small number of victims of rape and murder, has still not been paid to the victims.

The Complainants observe that the judgment of the Operational Military Court in the DRC is arbitrary because even if it had been served on the victims or their lawyers, it would not have been open to appeal or objection in accordance with Article 87 of Law No. 023/2002 of 18 November 2002 on the Military Judicial Code, which provides that "Judgments delivered by the Operational Military Courts are not open to any remedy". According to the Complainants, the position of the Military Judicial Code is reinforced by the Presidential Order which established and authorised ex officio this Operational Court in the operational zones of North Kivu. They allege that this Congolese legislation deprives the victims of the right of recourse against decisions rendered by operational military courts.

The Complainants allege the violation of the right to property. In support of this allegation, the Complainants argue that the FARDC committed looting of property in shops and ransacked and destroyed houses and dwellings, thereby depriving the victims of their homes and belongings. They stress that along their path, the FARDC looted the victims' small livestock, food, clothes, mattresses, crops, firewood, dishes, merchandise, small savings or stocks.

The Complainants further allege that the FARDC destroyed any property found on their path, committing in particular acts of extortion, malicious destruction, damage or deterioration of fields and property, destruction of kiosks whose contents were carried off, as well as extortion of sums of money. They argue that these acts infringed the right to property of the affected populations.

The Complainants allege the violation of the right to the protection of physical and mental health. They point out that the violations committed against them by FARDC elements had serious consequences for their health. They argue, with psychologists' reports in support, that those among them who benefited from being heard by psychologists revealed post-traumatic disorders.

The Complainants state that those who were subjected to rape, especially gang rape by soldiers, suffered complications of their genital organs while others still suffer from incurable sexually transmitted diseases. Others became pregnant, had abortions with many perinatal and postnatal complications, which endangered their sexual health.

The Complainants report the lack of access to care because the theft and systematic looting of their property plunged them into destitution without the possibility of paying the fees necessary for medical and psychological care in health facilities which, moreover, are not close to the victims.

The Complainants allege the absence of medical and psychological care for the victims of Minova by the Congolese State although it was informed of their fate by Judgment RP003/2013 delivered by the Congolese military courts and not open to appeal. Moreover, the Congolese State has adopted no measure to provide medication to the victims who are still ill because of the violations committed by its army.

The Complainants allege that, by their acts of looting along their path in the locality of Minova and its surroundings, the FARDC caused a general impoverishment of the victims and their families. No longer able to feed themselves and their families, this situation of poverty, coupled with the absence of housing and adequate sanitation means, because they were destroyed by the FARDC, makes their health even more vulnerable and they are regularly exposed to diseases.

Not only do such victims experience daily the psychological trauma of being called "soldiers' wives", but above all the Congolese State has to date adopted no measure to relieve the victims with regard to their sexual and reproductive health. The prevalence of poverty, economic dependence, the experience of violence as well as prejudices in the community and in society as a whole only aggravate the already unbearable health situation of the victims.

In the Complainants' understanding, the Respondent State violated the provisions of Article 1 of the Charter. They argue the failure of the Respondent State to adopt adequate measures to prevent the violation of the rights that the Charter enshrines, failing which it is bound to give justice to the victims and make reparation for the harm caused to them.

The Complainants consider that, taking into account the violation of the provisions of Article 5 of the African Charter and Article 3.1 of the Protocol to the African Charter on the Rights of Women; of Article 6 of the African Charter and Article 4 (1) and (2) (a) and (e) of the Maputo Protocol; of Article 7(1) of the African Charter; of Article 14 of the African Charter and Article 19 (c) of the Maputo Protocol, the violation of Article 1 of the African Charter is established as of right against the DRC.

As the procedure indicates, the Respondent State has not responded to the Complainants' observations on the merits despite the Notes Verbales sent to it and the time limits granted to it for that purpose in accordance with the relevant provisions of the Commission's Rules of Procedure.

In its practice, the Commission may render a decision by default where the Respondent State has not submitted its observations at the expiry of the required time limits. On the basis of its jurisprudence and the findings made in the procedure, the Commission so decides as regards the merits of the present Communication.

The Commission observes that the present communication is based on a case alleging violations some of which are similar to Communication 686/18 - Association of Women Lawyers Defenders of Human Rights, Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa & Equality Now v. Democratic Republic of the Congo. Consequently, the decision taken in that case served as a reference for the drafting of the Communication under consideration because the two are aligned on certain similar factual and legal positions. They also present the same types of requests for reparation.

Before examining the Complainants' allegations on the merits, it is important for the Commission to establish the scope of its competence under the Charter but also to interpret the Maputo Protocol. Indeed, in the present Communication, in addition to the allegations of violations of the African Charter, the Complainants invite the Commission to find the violation of the provisions of the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights on the Rights of Women in Africa (the Maputo Protocol). It is therefore incumbent on the Commission to verify its competence to interpret this Protocol.

Article 27 of the Maputo Protocol on its interpretation states that "the African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights shall be seized with matters of interpretation arising from the application or implementation of this Protocol". This provision implies that, in the event of a conflict of interpretation of the Maputo Protocol, it is the Court that is competent to decide. However, this does not mean that the Commission is not competent to interpret this instrument for the protection of women's rights in Africa.

In its jurisprudence, the Commission has already concluded that by its expression "Protocol to the Charter", the Maputo Protocol is a supplement and, consequently, forms an integral part of the African Charter. This even results from Article 66 of the Charter, which provides for the adoption of special protocols or agreements, if necessary, to "supplement the provisions of the present Charter". In particular, the Maputo Protocol finds its raison d'être or legal basis in the provisions of Article 18(3) of the Charter, which requires all States to eliminate every discrimination against women and to ensure the protection of the rights of women as stipulated in international declarations and conventions. It therefore supplements the Charter in its Article 18(3).

The status of the Maputo Protocol as a supplement to the Charter can also be deduced from its Article 26, which requires States to include in their periodic reports submitted in accordance with Article 62 of the African Charter, indications of the legislative and other measures they have undertaken for the full realisation of the rights recognised in the Maputo Protocol.

Thus, as the Commission is vested with the power to interpret the principal instrument, the Charter, it follows that it is also vested with it for the protocol attached to it, in this case, the Maputo Protocol.

In addition to the arguments and requests developed at the stage of seizure, the Commission notes that in their submissions on the merits, the Complainants did not submit arguments on the violation of Articles 4 and 15 of the African Charter and Articles 8, 11, 24 and 25 of the Maputo Protocol. In this regard, the Commission cannot rule on them for lack of submission of the relevant arguments and evidence by the Complainants.

The Commission further notes that the Complainants allege the violation of Articles 16 and 19 of the Maputo Protocol. As these additional arguments are the subject of new requests, the Commission must rule on them prior to the examination on the merits. In this regard, the Commission has already observed that additional substantive submissions are admissible provided that they are not based on new facts, do not call into question matters settled at the admissibility stage, that their author can substantiate them and that the opposing party cannot successfully contest them.

On the facts, the Commission notes that they do not vary between the seizure, admissibility and the merits, except that the Complainants point to the links between the violated articles of the African Charter and those of the Maputo Protocol, in accordance with the violations committed against women, who moreover constitute the majority of the victims in the present Communication. The facts on which the arguments based on the violation of Articles 16 and 19 of the Maputo Protocol are founded cannot therefore be considered new.

As regards the fulfilment of the admissibility requirements, the facts underlying the allegations of violation of Articles 16 and 19 of the Maputo Protocol are intimately linked to those reported concerning the violation of Article 14 of the African Charter. Indeed, the facts alleged at the stage of seizure and admissibility and relating to the violation of the right to property were the subject of remedies before the domestic courts.

In consequence of the foregoing, the Commission receives the Complainants in these additional arguments and requests. As to the examination on the merits, the Commission notes that the arguments based on the violation of Article 14 of the Charter provide detailed and complete information on the violation of Articles 16 and 19 of the Maputo Protocol. The Commission is of the view that the arguments based on the violation of Articles 16 and 19 of the Maputo Protocol should also be examined.

Under the provisions of Article 5 of the Charter, "Every individual shall have the right to the respect of the dignity inherent in a human being and to the recognition of his legal status. All forms of exploitation and degradation of man particularly slavery, slave trade, torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment and treatment shall be prohibited". Article 3(1) of the Maputo Protocol provides for its part that "Every woman shall have the right to dignity inherent in a human being and to the recognition and protection of her human and legal rights".

The Commission observes that the two provisions are interconnected and complement each other in that they both contribute to respect for human dignity. Indeed, while Article 5 advocates respect for the dignity of every individual, Article 3(1) of the Protocol is specific because it advocates the dignity of women. Article 5 of the Charter lists certain attitudes that lead to the violation of human dignity including, among others, torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment or treatment, which are alleged by the Complainants in the present communication.

In its relevant jurisprudence, the Commission has already established a connection in principle between torture, inhuman and degrading treatment and human dignity. This is so, among others, in the cases of Modise v. Botswana and Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights and Interights v. Egypt where the Commission considers that inhuman and degrading treatment necessarily violates human dignity.

Neither the Charter nor the Maputo Protocol defines the notion of torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment or treatment. In the absence of such a definition in the Charter, the Commission can only draw inspiration from other international human rights instruments pursuant to Articles 60 and 61 of the Charter. Thus, in its jurisprudence on torture and inhuman treatment, the Commission adopts the definition of the United Nations Committee against Torture, which observes that to be characterised as torture, the acts perpetrated must not only be severe pain or suffering, but above all caused by or at the instigation of a public authority, with the aim of punishing or obtaining information or a confession, such pain or suffering being physical or mental.

As to the notion of "cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment or treatment", the Commission stressed in the case of Media Rights v. Nigeria that "the expression 'cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment and treatment' is to be interpreted so as to extend to the widest possible protection against abuses, whether physical or mental".

On the arguments based on the violation of the above-mentioned provisions, the Complainants seek to have it concluded that gang rape, attacks against civilian populations and sexual violence constitute torture within the meaning of the Convention against Torture. They also point out that the systematic looting of houses, kiosks and livestock; the extortion and malicious destruction of property, large-scale armed robbery, the illegal occupation of land belonging to communities, as well as the damage of fields and dwellings infringe the dignity of the victims.

In the present case, the Complainants' submissions, the victims' testimonies and the reports from psychologists made available to the Commission prove that physical and mental violence was indeed inflicted on the victims. The Commission notes that the reports on the psycho-clinical expert assessment of the victims of the sexual violence in Minova drawn up by the clinical psychologists Mufungizi Bahati Olivier and Malumalu Machozi Pharailde-Céline and signed respectively on 3/10/2022 and 24/09/2022 notably describe the sequences of acts of gang rape, sexual violence and attacks committed by the FARDC against civilian populations.

In its General Comment No. 4, the Commission expressly referred to acts of sexual and gender-based violence as a form of torture and ill-treatment because of the specific, traumatic and gender-specific impact of sexual violence on victims, including at the individual, family and collective levels.

The Commission notes that these acts were inflicted by a public authority, namely the FARDC. The Commission is also of the view, with the Complainants, that these acts were intentional, because it is manifest that the perpetrators (that is, the FARDC) committed these abuses and atrocities against the civilian populations after their humiliation in the face of the advance of the M23 fighters.

It follows that all the conditions are met to conclude that there was torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment and, consequently, an infringement of the human dignity of the victims. It is therefore appropriate to conclude that the Respondent State violated the provisions of Articles 5 of the African Charter and 3 (1) of the Maputo Protocol.

Article 6 of the Charter, which stipulates that: "Every individual shall have the right to liberty and to the security of his person. No one may be deprived of his freedom except for reasons and conditions previously laid down by law. In particular, no one may be arbitrarily arrested or detained". The provisions of this article protect both the right to liberty of the person and the right to security of the person.

Indeed, the enjoyment of these two rights plays an important role in that it influences the enjoyment of other rights. This was, moreover, stressed by the United Nations Human Rights Committee in its General Comment No. 35, indicating that liberty and security of person are precious in themselves and also because the deprivation of liberty and the denial of security of person have historically been means of impairing the enjoyment of other rights.

In analysing the first component relating to the right to liberty, the Commission indicated, in the case of Amnesty International and others v. Sudan, that at the heart of the right to liberty lies the guarantee that no one may be deprived of the freedom to go or not to go wherever he or she wishes, provided that he or she has the power and the means to do so.

In the present Communication, the Commission notes that the generalised insecurity in Minova and its surroundings was sown by the relentlessness of the FARDC against the populations, some of whom were forced to flee their homes because the soldiers began to destroy and loot everything on their path following their defeat by the M23. Most of the victims, including women and girls, were forced to stay in their homes where they were subjected to sexual violence including gang rapes.

The Commission further notes that if the populations cannot go or move freely, because of insecurity or because their homes have been destroyed, their freedom is proscribed. The responsibility for the violation lies with the Respondent State, which did not take appropriate measures to protect the right to liberty of its citizens against the abuses committed by the FARDC. Accordingly, the Commission concludes that the restriction on the victims' liberty violates Article 6 of the Charter.

The second part of the Commission's analysis concerns the notion of "security of person". The scope of this notion is broader than that of the mere protection of an individual's liberty. The Human Rights Committee has considered that the right to security of person obliges a State Party not to ignore threats to the personal security of persons, detained or non-detained, within its jurisdiction. The State cannot ignore threats to the lives of persons within its jurisdiction just because those persons are not arrested or otherwise detained. The State should rather take reasonable and appropriate measures to protect all individuals.

In Communication Sudan Human Rights Organisation and Centre on Housing Rights v. Sudan, the Commission ruled clearly on the meaning of the right to security of person when it stated that the latter can be considered as an extension of rights based on the prohibitions of torture and cruel and unusual punishment. The right to security of person includes in particular the security of the nation and of the individual. National security examines how the State protects the physical integrity of its citizens against threats from outside such as invasion, terrorism and bio-security risks to human health. The security of the individual, on the other hand, can be viewed from two different angles: public security and private security. For public security, the law examines how the State protects the physical integrity of its citizens against abuses by official authorities and for private security, the law examines how the State protects the physical integrity of its citizens from abuses by other citizens (third parties or non-State actors).

On the argument based on the violation of the right to security of person, the Commission notes that the government of the Respondent State left the populations of Minova and its surroundings at the mercy of the barbaric acts of the FARDC, which not only failed to protect civilians but themselves subjected them to violations and abuses of all kinds. It further notes that the civilian populations suffered brutalities such as rape including gang rape, the looting and destruction of houses, fields and property.

In view of these facts, the Commission considers that the State has not complied with its obligations to ensure the security of its citizens by failing to protect them against the abuses and atrocities of the FARDC, who freely and with impunity violated the rights of the populations they were supposed to protect. It must therefore be concluded that Article 6 of the Charter was violated.

Article 4 (1) of the Maputo Protocol stipulates that "Every woman shall be entitled to respect for her life and the integrity and security of her person. All forms of exploitation, cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment and treatment shall be prohibited". This provision protects the right to life, to physical integrity and to the security of women.

The United Nations Human Rights Committee has stressed that "the right to life concerns the entitlement of individuals to be free from acts and omissions that are intended or may be expected to cause their unnatural or premature death, as well as to enjoy a life with dignity". As to physical integrity, the Commission considers that it is impaired when acts of torture, inhuman or degrading treatment or any kind of barbarity are inflicted on a human being. This implies that respect for physical integrity ensures the protection of the human body and of human life. The right to human security, for its part, protects the human person against any serious and widespread threat.

Thus, through its Article 4 (1), the Maputo Protocol requires that the life, physical integrity and security of women be respected in all respects. As the Commission has already indicated in the case of Geneviève Mbiankeu v. Cameroon, States are bound not only by the obligation to respect the rights of their citizens but also to protect them against violation by third parties. Thus, in the case of World Organisation Against Torture and League of the Africa Zone for the Defence of the Rights of Children and Pupils (on behalf of Céline) v. Democratic Republic of the Congo, the Commission considered that the acts of physical violence and gang rape perpetrated against the victim undoubtedly constitute a violation of her physical and moral integrity.

In the present communication, as demonstrated above, the victims faced acts of torture and cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment resulting from the gang rapes inflicted on them. This constitutes an infringement of their security and physical integrity. The Commission concludes that the provisions of Article 4 (1) of the Maputo Protocol have been violated.

Article 7 (1) provides: "1. Every individual shall have the right to have his cause heard. This comprises: (a) the right to an appeal to competent national organs against acts of violating his fundamental rights as recognized and guaranteed by conventions, laws, regulations and customs in force; (b) the right to be presumed innocent until proved guilty by a competent court or tribunal; (c) the right to defence, including the right to be defended by counsel of his choice; (d) the right to be tried within a reasonable time by an impartial court or tribunal."

In the case of Kevin Mgwanga Gunme et al v. Cameroon, the Commission indicated that respect for the rights set out in Article 7 is a fundamental principle in any democratic State. It considers that it is through respect for these rights that the other rights guaranteed by the Charter can be realised. Thus, it is important that States take rigorous measures to ensure their implementation or to allow their observance.

On the arguments based on the violation of the provisions of Article 7(1) of the Charter, the arguments advanced by the Complainants seek to have it concluded that there was a violation of the right to impartial justice owing to the failure to prosecute all the alleged perpetrators, the failure to notify the victims and their lawyers of the date of delivery of the judgment as well as the failure to serve the decision rendered at last instance.

The Commission considers that impartiality can be understood as the absence of prejudice or bias on the part of the judge in examining the case brought before him or her. In light of the Commission's relevant jurisprudence, impartiality covers internal and external elements relating both to the judge himself or herself and to other authorities having competence in the organisation of the judicial system.

The European Court of Human Rights rules more fully on the question, concluding that the principle covers both the subjective impartiality of the judge and the objective impartiality of the tribunal. While the former is linked to the personal conviction of the judge, the latter is based on the alleged or actual bias of the court. In sum, the aim is to guarantee an apparent impartiality, the proof of which falls on the party alleging it.

In the case under examination, the Commission notes that the Military Prosecutor's Offices of South and North Kivu charged, in their single pre-trial investigation, only 39 soldiers out of approximately 8000 soldiers who had taken part in the operations that led to the facts and violations that are the subject of the present Communication.

The Commission observes that the pre-trial investigation and the judgment of the Operational Military Court constitute tangible proof of the lack of objectivity of the bodies concerned with regard to the human rights violations committed by the FARDC in Minova and its surroundings. The Commission notes that of the 39 alleged perpetrators prosecuted, the Operational Military Court pronounced only 16 convictions, incriminating certain rank-and-file soldiers. It further notes that 14 high-ranking officers who bore responsibility as superiors of the troops in the localities covered by the communication as well as 9 other junior officers who had also been charged with serious acts of systematic sexual violence were all acquitted despite the confessions of some of them during their hearings and the testimonies of the victims.

The Commission observes that the victims and their lawyers were not notified of the date of delivery of the judgment nor did they receive notification of the decision rendered in the case concerning them. It also notes that to date the victims have not received the compensation that the judgment delivered awarded to them.

On the argument based on the arbitrary nature of the judgment rendered by the Operational Military Court owing to the fact that it is open neither to appeal nor to objection in accordance with Law No. 023/2002 of 18 November 2002 on the Judicial Code, the Commission, having already concluded that the court seized was partial, considers that there is no longer any need to examine the arbitrary nature of the decision rendered.
On the strength of all these grounds, the Commission concludes that the Operational Military Court was partial and consequently that the provisions of Article 7(1)(d) of the Charter were violated.

This article provides that "The right to property shall be guaranteed. It may only be encroached upon in the interest of public need or in the general interest of the community and in accordance with the provisions of appropriate laws".

In its jurisprudence on the right to property, the Commission has not defined property and its exhaustive content under the provisions of Article 14 of the Charter. It has, however, concluded in the case of Malawi African Association and others v. Mauritania that a plot of land and any structure erected on it constitute property under the provisions of Article 14 of the Charter. The Commission also observed in the case of IHRDA v. Angola that television sets, shoes, wristwatches and clothes are goods considered as property within the meaning of Article 14 of the Charter.

Still in its jurisprudence, the Commission has also observed that the "right to property" includes not only the right to have access to one's property and not to have one's property encroached upon or invaded, but also the right to own, use and control that property without hindrance, as the owner or owners see fit.

The African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights also recalled in the case of ACHPR v. Kenya that the right to property in its classical meaning includes the right to use the thing that is its object (usus), the right to enjoy its fruits (fructus) and the right to dispose of it (abusus).

The Commission has already observed that Article 14 of the Charter establishes two aspects of the right to property. The first is of a general nature: it is the principle of property and the peaceful enjoyment of property. The second principle concerns the possibility of deprivation of the right to property by public need or the general interest, limitations left to the relevant national legislation to define.

On examining the arguments invoked, the Commission notes that the acts of destruction of houses, extortion and looting of property by the FARDC do not constitute the legitimate deprivations provided for under the provisions of Article 14 of the Charter. Thus, the Commission concludes that the right to property guaranteed by Article 14 of the Charter has been violated in all its aspects. On the violation of Article 16 of the Maputo Protocol

Article 16 of the Maputo Protocol provides that: "Women shall have the right to equal access to housing and to acceptable living conditions in a healthy environment. To ensure this right, States Parties shall grant to women, whatever their marital status, access to adequate housing". This article protects the right to housing for women on an equal footing with men.

In its Principles and Guidelines on the Implementation of Economic, Social and Cultural Rights in the African Charter, the Commission defined the human right to adequate housing as "the right of everyone to gain and sustain a safe and secure home and community in which to live in peace and dignity". In the SERAC case, the Commission indicated that, at the very minimum, the right to housing obliged the Nigerian government not to destroy the houses of its citizens.

It thus considered that the obligation to respect housing rights requires that the State, and therefore all its organs and agents, abstain from carrying out, sponsoring or tolerating any practice, policy or legal measure violating the integrity of the individual or infringing upon their freedom to use these materials or other resources available to them, in a way they find most appropriate to satisfy individual, family, household or community housing needs. Within the meaning of Article 16 of the Maputo Protocol, women must be protected against such practices, policies and legal measures that block the use of their homes in any way.

As explained in the SERAC case, the right to housing goes even further than a roof over one's head and encompasses the right of every individual to be left alone and to live in peace whether under a roof or not. In the present case, it results from the Complainants' submissions that some of the victims' houses were destroyed and ransacked. As indicated above, all these acts violate the right to housing. The Commission therefore concludes that Article 16 of the Maputo Protocol has been violated.

Article 19 (c) of the Maputo Protocol obliges all States Parties to take all appropriate measures to promote women's access to and control over productive resources such as land and to guarantee their right to property. This article protects one of the aspects of the right to sustainable development of women in Africa. It aims in particular at the promotion of the economic rights and independence of women.

This provision invites States to contribute to facilitating the independent development of women and, consequently, to enable their economic potential. They must, in particular, make available to them the productive resources necessary for their economic fulfilment.

In the present case, the Commission observes that a number of items of property belonging to the victims were destroyed or looted. These include in particular houses and many other effects they contained. The testimonies show in particular that systematic looting of houses and kiosks, theft of livestock, property and money; extortion and wilful destruction of property, characterised the attacks perpetrated by the soldiers. The Commission considers that all these effects constitute productive resources for the victims and concludes that the Respondent State was not able to protect them. It finds the consequent violation of Article 19 (c) of the Maputo Protocol by the Respondent State.

Article 16 of the Charter stipulates that: "1. Every individual shall have the right to enjoy the best attainable state of physical and mental health. 2. States Parties to the present Charter shall take the necessary measures to protect the health of their people and to ensure that they receive medical attention when they are sick."

The Commission has observed that the right to the best attainable state of health includes the right to health facilities, access to goods and services which must be guaranteed to all, without discrimination of any kind. In reality, the right to the best attainable state of health means the existence of health care, services and conditions, their accessibility, acceptability and quality and imposes on the State the duty to respect, fulfil and protect it. These care, services and conditions include, among others, as explained by the Commission in the Pretoria Declaration on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights in Africa, health services accessible to all, access to the minimum of food necessary to avoid malnutrition, access to housing, to safe drinking water, to reproductive health and to protection against most infectious diseases.

In the case of Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights and INTERIGHTS v. Egypt, the Commission noted that the right to health functions directly or indirectly as a precondition to all the other human rights recognised by the African Charter. This was also stressed in Communication Purohit and Moore v. The Gambia in which the Commission indicated that the enjoyment of the right to health as widely understood is vital to all aspects of a person's life and well-being, and is crucial to the realisation of all the other fundamental human rights and freedoms.

The Commission also indicated in its Principles and Guidelines on the Implementation of Economic, Social and Cultural Rights in the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights that the right to health also includes the right to be free from unjustified interference, including, among others, the right not to be subjected to torture and other forms of ill-treatment. What is more, in the same principles and guidelines, the Commission indicated that one of the minimum core obligations of the right to health is to prevent violence against women and mitigate its impact on the physical and mental health of survivors.

In the present case, as already explained above, the victims were subjected to torture and other inhuman and degrading treatment. In this sense, the Commission considers that this constitutes an infringement of the right to health within the meaning of Article 16 of the Charter. In particular, the Commission observes that the gang rapes perpetrated by the FARDC on victims in the presence of their parents, husbands or children caused indelible physical, moral and psychological after-effects and, for some, sexually transmitted diseases.

The Commission also notes that in the present case, the victims' right to health prescribed by the above-mentioned provisions was necessarily compromised by the lack of housing following the destruction of their houses but also the impoverishment of families because of the looting committed by the FARDC.

The Commission further notes that the Respondent State did nothing to prevent these acts or mitigate their impact on the physical or mental health of the victims.
